result.markdown: --- title: "The standard error, derived in bands" description: "Casella and Berger get Var(X-bar) = sigma squared over n from one expansion and one substitution. Here every equation carries its own numbered R line, in six bands — and 100,000 simulated samples check the result at the end." date: 2026-08-10 categories: - book-revisions tags: - standard error - variance - independence engine: knitr code-summary: "Show the working" --- ## Claim The standard error of a mean is a number you can derive without imagining a second sample. Casella and Berger do it in §5.2: Theorem 5.2.6(b), p. 214, proves $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\sigma^2/n$, and the standard error is its square root. The proof has one idea, and it is not a clever one. Square the deviation, expand the square into $n^2$ terms, then take the expectation of the right-hand side term by term: the $n$ squared terms each expect $\sigma^2$, and independence forces all $n(n-1)$ cross terms to expect zero. What survives is $n\sigma^2$. Divide by $n^2$ and the $n$ cancels once, leaving $\sigma^2/n$. Everything below is that sentence, with one numbered line of R beside each equation. No step of the derivation is estimated, and no distribution is assumed — the simulation appears in the last band only, and only to check the answer the algebra already gave. ## What it means in English You took twenty-five measurements and averaged them. The average is not the truth; it is off by *something*, and the standard error says how big that something usually is. A spread of 1.3 cm per measurement becomes 0.26 cm of error in the average of twenty-five — a factor of 5 smaller, because $\sqrt{25}=5$. Four things it is not: - **Not the standard deviation of your measurements.** That is 1.3 cm, and collecting more data leaves it where it is. The standard error is what shrinks. - **Not the variance of the mean.** That is 0.0676, in cm². It is the standard error squared, and it is not an error bar. - **Not a probability.** On its own it is a distance. It becomes "95 per cent of the time" only once you know the shape of the scatter. - **Not something the simulation at the end proves.** The simulation is a check on arithmetic that is already finished. Delete band 6 and the theorem still stands. ## Code, maths, English Six bands. Inside a band, each code line `L` has exactly one equation `(b.n)` beside it and each equation has exactly one code line, so the map column reads `L4 ↔ (2.1)` in both directions. Definitions are labelled as definitions: where a pair is an assignment rather than a probability statement, the maths uses $:=$ and the comment says so. ::: {.transition} | Code | Maths | English | |:--|:--|:--| | **BAND 1 — the three numbers** | | | | **L1 ↔ (1.1)** `mu <- 5` | (1.1) $\mu := 5$ | A definition, not a measurement. R's `<-` and maths' $:=$ are the same statement, in two alphabets. | | **L2 ↔ (1.2)** `sigma <- 1.3` | (1.2) $\sigma := 1.3,\quad\sigma^2 = 1.69$ | 1.3 cm is one measurement's spread. 1.69 is the same fact squared, in cm². They differ by a square root, and that difference is the whole post. | | **L3 ↔ (1.3)** `n <- 25` | (1.3) $n := 25$ | How many measurements. Fixed by design, not estimated from anything. | | **BAND 2 — one sample, and its deviations** | | | | **L4 ↔ (2.1)** `x <- rnorm(n, mu, sigma)` | (2.1) $X_1,\dots,X_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ | 25 draws. The normal is a convenient source of independent numbers and nothing more: no later line uses its shape. | | **L5 ↔ (2.2)** `z <- x - mu` | (2.2) $z_i := X_i - \mu,\qquad E[z_i] = 0$ | Centre each measurement on the truth. After this line $\mu$ is gone and only $z$ remains, which is why every later step is short. Note $z$ is centred on the **truth**, not on `mean(x)`. | | **BAND 3 — the square splits into two blocks** | | | | **L6 ↔ (3.1)** `M <- outer(z, z)` | (3.1) $\Big(\sum_i z_i\Big)^2 = \sum_i z_i^2 + \sum_{i\ne j} z_i z_j$ | Every product of two deviations, all 625 of them, in one 25×25 matrix. | | **L7 ↔ (3.2)** `sum(diag(M))` | (3.2) $\sum_i z_i^2 \quad$ — $n$ diagonal terms | prints 66.76. That is *this* sample's diagonal block. Hold on to it: band 4 will print something else, and both will be correct. | | **L8 ↔ (3.3)** `sum(M) - sum(diag(M))` | (3.3) $\sum_{i\ne j} z_i z_j \quad$ — $n(n-1)$ cross terms | prints 160.7. And 66.76 + 160.7 = 227.4, which is $(\sum z_i)^2$. The split is exact, not approximate. | | **L9 ↔ (3.4)** `n + n * (n - 1)` | (3.4) $n + n(n-1) = n^2$ | prints 625 — the count, matching the matrix's 625 cells. $n$ squares and $n(n-1)$ crosses, nothing else. | | **BAND 4 — take the expectation of each block** | | | | **L10 ↔ (4.1)** `S <- matrix(rnorm(N * n, mu, sigma), N, n) - mu` | (4.1) $N$ independent samples of size $n$, each centred the same way | 100,000 repeats of band 2. This is what "expectation" means when you have to compute it: the same experiment, many times, averaged. | | **L11 ↔ (4.2)** `mean(rowSums(S^2))` | (4.2) $E\Big[\sum_i z_i^2\Big] = n\sigma^2$ | prints 42.28 ± 0.03782, against $n\sigma^2 = 42.25$. **This is why L7's 66.76 was not an error**: one sample varies, the average over 100,000 does not. Band 4 exists to make that difference undeniable. | | **L12 ↔ (4.3)** `mean(rowSums(S)^2 - rowSums(S^2))` | (4.3) $E[z_iz_j] = \operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j) = 0,\quad i \ne j$ | prints 0.04796 ± 0.1851 against an exact 0. Zero plus noise. This single line is where independence is used — forget it and the block is a covariance, and the answer is no longer $\sigma^2/n$. | | **L13 ↔ (4.4)** `n * sigma^2` | (4.4) $n\sigma^2 = 42.25$ | The exact value L11 was aiming at. No draws, no noise: this is what the algebra delivers before any data exists. | | **BAND 5 — add the blocks, divide by $n^2$, then root** | | | | **L14 ↔ (5.1)** `(1 / n^2) * (n * sigma^2)` | (5.1) $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X) = \dfrac{1}{n^2}\,n\sigma^2 = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}$ | prints 0.0676, in **cm²**. The two blocks went back together: $n\sigma^2 + 0 = 42.25$, then the $1/n^2$ out front, and one $n$ cancels. That cancellation is Theorem 5.2.6(b). | | **L15 ↔ (5.2)** `sigma / sqrt(n)` | (5.2) $\operatorname{SE}(\bar X) = \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$ | prints 0.26, in **cm**. Not the same number as (5.1) and not interchangeable with it: one is the other squared. If (5.1) and (5.2) ever look like the same quantity, the units have stopped doing their job. | | **BAND 6 — check the finished result by simulation** | | | | **L16 ↔ (6.1)** `means <- replicate(N, mean(rnorm(n, mu, sigma)))` | (6.1) $\bar X_1,\dots,\bar X_N$ from $N$ independent samples | 100,000 averages, each from 25 fresh measurements. This is the experiment the theorem makes a prediction about, run 100,000 times. | | **L17 ↔ (6.2)** `var(means)` | (6.2) $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X) \approx \widehat{\operatorname{var}}\big(\{\bar X_k\}\big)$ | prints 0.06734 against the exact 0.0676 — ratio 0.9962. The variance of the averages lands on (5.1). | | **L18 ↔ (6.3)** `sd(means)` | (6.3) $\operatorname{SE}(\bar X) \approx \widehat{\operatorname{sd}}\big(\{\bar X_k\}\big)$ | prints 0.2595 against the exact 0.26. Rooting L17's answer, or taking the spread of the 100,000 means, gives the same number to three digits. | ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Where this comes from **The derivation.** Casella & Berger, *Statistical Inference*, 2nd ed., §5.2. Lemma 5.2.5 (p. 213) states $\operatorname{Var}\big(\sum g(X_i)\big)=n\operatorname{Var}g(X_1)$; its proof writes the variance as the expectation of a squared sum and counts $n$ diagonal and $n(n-1)$ cross terms. Theorem 4.5.5 makes each cross term a covariance; independence makes it zero. Theorem 5.2.6(b) (p. 214) takes $g(x)=x/n$, giving $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=n\cdot\sigma^2/n^2=\sigma^2/n$. Bands 2 to 5 are that proof with the expectations written out instead of cited, so that L12 is visibly the step where independence enters and nowhere else. **The name.** §5.2 stops at the variance. The words "standard error" do not occur until §10.1.4, "Bootstrap Standard Errors", p. 478. Taking the square root — (5.2) — is the step every applied text adds and this one does not. **The code.** One chunk, `include: false`, labelled `se-bands`. Every number in the table is pulled from it as an inline `r` expression formatted to four significant figures; none is typed. `set.seed(7)` fixes the single sample in bands 2 and 3, and `set.seed(11)` the 100,000 replicates in bands 4 and 6, so the printed values are stable across renders. **About the sample in band 3.** It is not typical, and it is not tuned. 66.76 against an expectation of 42.28 is roughly two standard deviations high. That gap is left in deliberately: it is the cleanest instance available of the difference between a realisation and its expectation, and a reader who has just seen both numbers in adjacent bands will not confuse them in band 5. **The photograph.** Carl Friedrich Gauss, 1840, by Christian Albrecht Jensen. A faithful photographic reproduction of a two-dimensional public-domain work; the artist died in 1870, and the painting is public domain in its country of origin and in the United States.
